 Dark Matter Season-Finale Recap: Into the Great Unknown
 By 
 Scott Tobias ,

 Photo: Apple TV 
 At the end of Dark Matter ’s first season, the many Jasons of the Jason-pocalyse were still stuck somewhere between the anger and bargaining phase of the five stages of grief, having blown past denial yet still too engaged in reconnecting with Daniela and Charlie to move forward. The standalone fifth episode of this season, “Love and Be Loved,” marked a pivotal shift through depression and acceptance, as one such Jason contemplated suicide before opting to get a fresh start in a world where Jason Dessen had died as a child, and his mother was still alive to welcome his miraculous return. Even then, it took more than a few dark nights of the soul for this Jason to work his way through the fog, surrender his ties to the recent past, and build a new life with someone else. When he meets the Daniela of that world and is able to exchange pleasantries with her before heading home to his new partner, acceptance has been achieved.
 And so now, in the final episode of the second season, one such Jason is able to have a conversation with Daniela as if they’ve gone through an amicable divorce years earlier and can reminisce about their history without falling into despair. This Jason is essentially escorting his wife through the box to find their son, but he’s resigned to the fact that there’s no getting either of them back. They laugh over a memory involving the twins when they were young, but Jason cuts the conversation short by opening the door to the world where he believes Charlie has landed. He rejects the idea of stepping through to see Charlie himself, because it’s not his role to play anymore. “It’s not fair to any of us, but we keep going,” he tells Daniela. “Thank you for a really great life.”
 The tone of these sorts of interactions has changed over the course of this season, as different people from different worlds have collided and been able to get past the impossibility of it. When Charlie No. 1 proved to Max that he was a multidimensional traveler and not his twin brother coming home early from college, what choice did Max have but believe him? And when Daniela No. 1 goes looking for her son and gets caught in the house by this world’s Daniela, the show doesn’t pause long to register this shocking revelation before it turns into a metaphysical therapy session. Daniela gets to tell some version of herself how she feels about her marital problems and her lingering guilt over having to kill one of the Jasons to protect her family. Often in life you need to be able to forgive yourself, but Daniela gets the rare opportunity to make that idea as literal as possible. It’s the sci-fi version of Stuart Smalley looking into the mirror and doing his daily affirmations.
 Though this season two finale is appropriately scaled up and exciting, with a lot of frantic action across multiple realities, the progression that Dark Matter has made to get to the acceptance phase of its premise raises an obvious question: Where could it go from here? There are some plot-related questions that will need to be answered next season — we’ll get to those in a bit — but there are signs in this last hour that Dark Matter has reached a potential dead end on an emotional and philosophical front. The impact of the two scenes with Daniela described above should be seismic given how much box-related upheaval she’s had to face since Jason No. 2 invaded her life. But this season, the show has reckoned so much with this type of emotional fallout that the scenes are feeling a little redundant and drippy. There’s no physical (or metaphysical) limit to where the series might go from here — the box does, after all, open up into infinite possible realities — but the door might have closed on a “Love and Be Loved”-type tearjerker again.
 On the other hand, perhaps the dramatic realignment of the major characters in the finale will open up other avenues. Heading toward season’s end, there appeared to be two camps working at cross purposes: Jason No. 1, Amanda No. 2, Ryan No. 1, and Blair No. 2 have been fussing over the science and logistics of destroying the box, starting from the original sources in World No. 2, because the boxes everywhere else would just respawn. Meanwhile, Leighton No. 2 and Jason No. 2 have been looking to refine their project through the Pyramid and perhaps return to the idealistic vision of addressing big problems with multi-dimensional solutions. But in an abrupt turn of events, Leighton No. 2 and Jason No. 2 start to regret this monstrous invention they’ve unleashed on humanity. Leighton talks about a world where Mt. Rainier had blown, leading to massive crop death and starvation, but the ecological solution he offered wound up deepening the crisis, starting with developing countries before spreading to the rest of the world.
 “We fucked up,” laments Leighton in a truly massive understatement. And in an even more surprising moment of self-awareness, he expresses regret over “letting millions of people die for money” and “walking around in awe of my own fucking greatness.” Jason No. 2 tries to ease the guilt that’s suddenly stabbing away at Leighton’s conscience by suggesting that the implications of the box were not knowable and “this thing has brought out the most terrifying aspects of who we are.” While it does seem a bit surprising that the Velocity braintrust didn’t think through the massive potential for disruption that the box would cause, it does track historically that scientists often think about what’s possible more than about where great advancements might lead humankind (see also: Oppenheimer ). Still, it’s a startling gearshift for all parties to come around on the idea that the box (and the Pyramid) might be worth shutting down.
 All parties, that is, except for Oluko, who has emerged as a late-breaking villain and ghost in the machine. Amanda No. 2 and Ryan No. 1 meet him at the Velocity building in Analog World with the intent of securing vaccines and medications to fight a plague in another dimension. But their true goal is to access the Analog World box in order to work back to the original box with the technology needed to “decohere” and destroy the entire system. Blair warns them that Oluko gave her “major creep vibes,” and indeed he sniffs out their intention and sends a security agent after them, leading to a splashy action sequence in which they’re being chased through multiple worlds, including one where Chicago has become a war zone. That sequence alone makes it seem like the show’s producers were saving the budgetary fireworks for the grand finale, just as last season ended with a rush of Jason-on-Jason violence.
 But once the dust has settled, Dark Matter lands in a tricky spot for next season. As hard as it was to get back to the original box in World No. 2, it appears that Blair No. 2 and Jason No. 1 succeeded in their de-coherence plan, but as with all box-related issues, the result is messier than anticipated. Oluko winds up escaping to some unknown world, leaving him as a looming threat, and more crucially, time runs out before Daniela and Charlie can make it back to Analog World for a family reunion. They open a door into an unknown future, but it’s obvious that they’ll need these dimensional portals to be opened up once again. The second season of Dark Matter has been a significant improvement on the first, but if the show gets a third — news on a renewal has yet to be announced — it will need to open that portal door, too, and find new possibilities.
 Infinite Jasons 
 • Blair offers some wonderful sci-fi nonsense in explaining how her gizmo will kill the box: “Basically it’ll attack not just the local qubits but all programming for the adaptive shielding, slowly corrupting the error-correcting protocols.” Adaptive shielding, error-correcting protocols. Got it.
 • Though the heart-tugging moments are not as potent in this episode as they were in earlier parts of the season, Daniela’s farewell to the grown-up version of Max she never knew is a killer. “It’s really nice to meet you” is a lovely bit of understatement.
 • Good on Charlie for going record shopping in Max’s world. Nirvana’s Bleach is a solid choice.
 • Oluko’s rise brings the first major character death in his doppelgänger, Leighton No. 2, whose murder ends up serving as a gruesome narrative sacrifice for his sins in exploiting the box.
